A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same benefit-of-personalization framework and retain identifiable theoretical and empirical material despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original MIMIC-III classification and regression experiments in Table 2, with subgroup distributions and feature-selection sensitivity analyses in Appendix G.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original UCI Heart and MIMIC-III Kidney evaluations using three explanation methods in Appendix G, Tables 4–5.

M1.justification: v2 generalizes the reliability audit to a practitioner-selected error tolerance v and revises the categorical and Laplace bounds used in that audit. The generic/personalized model comparison, group-cost differences, minimum-group aggregation, and empirical rejection rule remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained MIMIC-III length-of-stay tasks, v2 adds UCI Heart classification of disease presence and regression of exercise-induced ST depression. It also adds a kidney-injury cohort with mortality classification and regression of time to continuous renal replacement therapy. These introduce distinct clinical populations and prediction targets.

E2.justification: The model comparator remains the generic counterpart of each personalized model; neither version evaluates a competing personalization or auditing algorithm. The added DeepLIFT and Shapley Value Sampling methods are explanation backends used within the framework for sensitivity analysis.

E3.justification: v1 discusses rejection over varying epsilon values and conditional cutoffs. v2 adds a worked audit using epsilon = 0.002 for prediction and explanation and an error tolerance of 25%. The retained MIMIC-III experiment still uses the 70/30 split, output normalization, and 50% feature retention/removal; no training rerun is established.

E4.justification: v2 adds a systematic analysis of whether benefit/harm findings depend on the explanation method, comparing Integrated Gradients, DeepLIFT, and Shapley Value Sampling across the Heart and Kidney tasks. This substantially extends evidence beyond v1's single explainer. The original distribution-fit diagnostics and feature-count sensitivity plots are retained in Appendix F.

E5.justification: The reported testing error changes from the sum of Type I and Type II errors to their equal-prior average, with the illustrative cutoff correspondingly changing from 50% to 25%. This revises statistical error reporting and interpretation. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or empirical significance tests.

E6.justification: All original MIMIC-III Table 2 scores and subgroup counts are retained. Tables 4–5 add extensive prediction and explanation results for four additional tasks. v2 also reports new UCI feasibility thresholds, including 0.1156 for classification, and revises numerical attribute-limit examples under its revised error formulation; these are not performance gains on the original experiment.

T1.justification: v2 adds Theorems 4.2–4.3 on explanation harm and opposing subgroup effects without prediction changes. The former additive-model theorem becomes a more qualified, group-specific regressor result in Theorem 4.4 with a rewritten proof. The error-bound theory also gains mixture-hypothesis constructions, revised normalization and distributional derivations, and a new minimum-group-size condition in Corollary 5.3.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds extending personalization evaluation and allowing more attributes in regression. v2 foregrounds limits that can make personalization benefits statistically untestable and explicitly claims that unchanged prediction can accompany explanation harm and conflicting subgroup effects. This substantially expands and redirects the main contribution statements.

C2.justification: For unchanged Table 2 gains, v1 discusses rejecting the null for sufficiency below the empirical benefit cutoffs; v2 emphasizes that sufficiency cannot be reliably tested at its chosen epsilon = 0.002. Figure 3 also explicitly states that a low error lower bound does not establish reliability. New discussion connects epsilon to practical value and distinguishes explanation-method faithfulness from ground-truth feature importance.

D1.justification: v2 documents Captum implementations for the additional explainers and provides feature specifications for the new datasets, including pre-CRRT laboratory measurements and SOFA scores for the kidney cohort. Existing MIMIC-III split, encoding, normalization, and feature-removal details are largely relocated to Appendix F.1. Detailed architectures, training hyperparameters, and code-access instructions remain absent.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly credits the existing BoP definitions to Monteiro Paes et al. and distinguishes their general definitions from theory restricted to binary costs, refining v1's binary-classification-only characterization. Related work expands substantially through explanation disparities, clinical explanation use, multicalibration, algorithmic recourse, and attribution of the testing argument to Le Cam's framework.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, statistical discussion, and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten. v2 distinguishes group BoP from minimum-group BoP more explicitly, reorganizes the theoretical appendices, and presents the main case study as a four-step practitioner walkthrough.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a single-column layout, redraws Figure 1, splits and expands the former Figure 2 into appendix Figures 5–6, and adds workflow Figure 3 and theoretical Figures 7–8. Error plots receive revised axes and annotations, Table 2 becomes a side-by-side comparison, and Tables 4–5 add new result displays.

improvement.justification: v2 improves error normalization, attribution, and practical explanation while broadening empirical checks. However, new Appendix C.2 calls S = X binary despite continuous X and defines a nonbinary classifier; the categorical bound differs between Corollary D.3 and its derivation; and Table 5 reports negative aggregate and minimum regression prediction benefits despite every subgroup benefit being positive. These inconsistencies affect the added theoretical and empirical support, preventing a reliable judgment that the substantial benefits outweigh the new reliability problems.
